piezas.titulo: Voluntary physical activity and pharmacological treatment with the Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761 alleviate regional alterations in cerebral synaptic density and improve behavioral recovery after unilateral labyrinthectomy in the rat
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundUnilateral peripheral vestibular loss induces adaptive mechanisms of cerebral plasticity. The quantified Ginkgo biloba extract EGb 761® has been shown to enhance neural plasticity, and is used in the treatment of vertigo and dizziness. We here aimed to investigate, how voluntary physical training in a running wheel (RWT) and oral treatment with EGb 761® affect behavioral recovery and whole-brain synaptic density following chemical unilateral labyrinthectomy (cUL) in the rat.MethodsThirty-two Sprague Dawley rats were divided into 4 groups with different treatment regimens (group 1: control food; group 2: control food + RWT; group 3: EGb 761® food (75mg/day/kg body weight); group 4: EGb 761® food + RWT). All rats underwent a left-sided cUL by transtympanic injection of bupivacaine and p-arsanilic acid. Behavioral testing (scoring of nystagmus, postural asymmetry, head tilt, locomotion tracking in open field) was done weekly until 9 weeks (d63) after cUL. Serial [18F]UCB-H μPET imaging of synaptic density (targeting synaptic vesicular protein 2A) was performed before and up to 9 weeks post cUL. Images were whole-brain normalized and segmented based on Schiffer's atlas. Voxel-wise and regional changes of cerebral [18F]UCB-H uptake were compared across groups and time points.ResultsAll rats showed signs of acute vestibular syndrome following cUL. The EGb 761® + RWT group had a significantly faster and more complete improvement of postural asymmetry by week 5 post UL and a higher locomotor velocity thereafter than the control food group. Compared to baseline, at d63 post cUL the EGb 761® group showed the smalles reduction of synaptic density in the vestibular nuclei of−7.59 ± 7.0 % (vs.−20.37 ± 5.18% in control food group, p < 0.001). In contrast, at d63 post cUL the motor cortex displayed the highest relative gain of synaptic density in the control food group (6.6 ± 3.13 % vs. 0.19 ± 2.81% in the EGb 761® group, p < 0.001). All treatment groups showed an increase of synaptic density in the hippocampal area and the somatosensory cortex at weeks 1-3 post cUL compared to the control food group. The additive effect of EGb 761® and RWT was statistically confirmed in behavior and PET measurements.ConclusionsUnilateral labyrinthectomy induces loss of synaptic density in vestibulo-cerebellar networks, which can be partially reversed by EGb 761® treatment. Combined physical and EGb 761® treatment improves behavioral recovery from cUL most effectively, reinforcing the importance of multimodal treatment in acute vestibulopathies.

piezas.titulo: Agent Factory recap: Agent harnesses, shifting left, and autonomous coding
piezas.resumenOriginal: In this episode of The Agent Factory , we explore the reality of building with autonomous agents alongside Ryan Lopopolo, a software engineer at Google Cloud and the person who coined the term agent harness . From throwing out manual code editors to treating team collaboration like leveling up RPG stats, Ryan breaks down how grounding models in rich context and shifting interventions left unlocks high levels of agent autonomy. This post guides you through the key ideas from our conversation. Use it to quickly recap topics or dive deeper into specific segments with links and timestamps. The Agent Harness - What is it? Timestamp: [ 00:30 ] An AI agent as we're defining it here is a large language model (LLM) plus an agent harness . Think of the harness as everything wrapped around the LLM that isn't the model itself. For example, if you're working in Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash , Gemini Flash is the LLM and Google Antigravity is the harness. While an unassisted model can answer simple questions out of the box, it can't check live conditions or interact with your workspace on its own. When a user asks a question like "Why is the sky blue?" , an unassisted LLM can respond without issue. However, when asked a question like "Should I wear a raincoat today?" , the model can't answer on its own because it lacks the necessary data. The harness catches the intent, queries live weather tools, bundles that context back into the prompt, and hands it to the model to produce an informed answer. Ryan Lopopolo on agent harnesses and autonomous coding Tilde Thurium sat down with Ryan Lopopolo to discuss what it takes to run fully autonomous coding workflows in production. See the summary below! Coining the harness and writing zero production code Timestamp: [ 02:22 ] The term agent harness grew out of Ryan's extensive work on autonomous coding agents, culminating in a February 2026 essay on leveraging coding models in an agent-first world. Ryan shared that he hasn't opened a traditional code editor since May of last year, maintaining that streak through his transition into Google Cloud . In this paradigm, engineers no longer author or review individual lines of syntax; instead, they operate at the level of natural language specifications and inspect the final artifacts, such as pull requests, documents, and spreadsheets. Then they determine whether the end result meets organizational standards. Harness engineering is the study and the practice of putting a model into an environment where it can succeed. If you don't do that work, you end up doing what I call 'prompt and pray'. Ryan Lopopolo Context curation and lazy prompting Timestamp: [ 03:35 ] Upfront harness investment pays off by allowing engineers to become lazy prompters. When the repository contains structured documentation, clear interfaces, and discoverable tools, you do not need to paste walls of text into a prompt box every morning "I aspire to be an incredibly lazy prompter. If I have done the job to give the model the tools and context it needs to ground itself, I don't need to write a long prompt. It figures it out." The model uses its harness to pull relevant context, allowing it to navigate large codebases and execute complex tasks without oversight. Shifting left: engineering best practices as autonomous guardrails Timestamp: [ 05:00 ] When an agent fails, developers face a whole spectrum of interventions. The most common reflex is to fiddle with the prompt or retry, but that never scales across a team. "The simplest, smooth-brain, stupidest intervention I can think of is literally just: try my prompt again without changing anything else. But shifting left means moving interventions earlier into the development lifecycle where they are cheapest and automated: from prompts, to repo docs, to linters, to tests, and all the way to upstream evals." Instead of hoping the model guesses right on the next turn, shifting left embeds standards directly into the environment. Linters, tests, and AGENTS.md files act as durable memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, making sure the agent stays on the rails without needing constant hand-holding. Leveraging established tools and determinism Timestamp: [ 06:50 ] Agents shine when they're handed tools that already mirror patterns heavily represented in pre-training data. Pairing models with standard command-line interfaces moves reasoning into determinism, shifting the burden of context aggregation away from the model and onto reliable tools. Ryan also shared an environmental design trick for context efficiency: structuring markdown files so link anchors sit directly beneath their corresponding prose blocks rather than inline. This prevents context clutter and mitigates "lost in the middle" retrieval issues. Because Ryan operates exclusively by reviewing end-state artifacts, keeping documentation readable allows him to easily inspect execution runs: "I want to be able to look at the pull request and review it. If it made a bad decision, I need to know where it went off the rails so I can whack the agent on the head and make sure it does not make that same mistake again." Long horizons and expanding the agentic loop Timestamp: [ 09:45 ] The central challenge of harness engineering is ensuring that agents cohere over long time horizons. Because human organizations produce software through iterative refinement rather than single-shot prompts, agent workflows must mirror that cadence. Harness engineering uses tightly scoped, reviewable pull requests to narrow the agent's state space. Stacking these high-confidence changes end-to-end allows supervisors to gradually expand the loop size, building trust until agents can autonomously execute large-scale initiatives, including entire language migrations Curating agent teams like RPG stats Timestamp: [ 11:58 ] Rather than divvying up sprint tasks based on individual specialties, having a diverse team contribute to an agent turns it into a central producer of work that carries everyone's strengths. Ryan compared leveling up an agent's capabilities to building out a character sheet: "[It's like] building out the stats of your RPG character. I get a new person on the team who is a React architect and boom! The attention that they pay is able to bump out the stats in front-end architecture and performance." With that collective expertise baked into the environment, the agent can autonomously classify incoming work and activate the exact skills it needs on demand, operating as both a backend architect and a front-end specialist. Accruing leverage in tools, not custom harnesses Timestamp: [ 14:38 ] For developers wondering whether to build their own custom agent harness, Ryan offered clear advice: don't build one from scratch. Standard harnesses already provide the foundational primitives: file reading, grep search, and command execution. Over-scaffolding an agent with rigid, bespoke frameworks creates technical debt and leads to sunk-cost traps when frontier models advance. "If you focus all of your efforts on improving quality on tools and context, you can freely adopt the newest models as they come out and you'll be constantly accruing leverage into a bit of the system that will never become obsolete." Operating Google Cloud and eliminating capability overhang Timestamp: [ 16:47 ] Discussing his work at Google Cloud , Ryan outlined his motivation to eliminate capability overhang : the delta between what frontier AI models are theoretically capable of and how much useful work is currently extracted in production. Because the cloud functions as a massive, programmable surface, equipping agents with direct interfaces to Google Cloud lets them manage and deploy infrastructure effectively, turning raw model capability into tangible enterprise utility. Continually updating your priors on AI Timestamp: [ 18:13 ] The speed of AI development requires engineers and teams to actively unlearn old limitations and constantly reassess what these models can achieve. " It's very important to continually be updating what you think is possible with these lovely tools that we have ," Ryan urged. What broke six months ago often runs effortlessly on today's frontier models. Rather than getting locked into rigid workflows, developers should build around the two highly extensible interfaces that will remain relevant across every model upgrade: tools and context. "Agents will always need context in order to do that last mile adaptation into what you think good is. And as you can continue to... shift it to the left, in terms of increasingly capable tools which act as a form of memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, you'll continually be amazed as the models are able to do more and more interesting things for you over time." How To Build A Custom Harness Next, Billy Jacobson started us off by showing how developers can customize their own agent harnesses for specific tasks. Under the hood: Why build a custom harness? Timestamp: [ 19:44 ] Before jumping into code, Billy unpacked why developers should understand the mechanics of a harness rather than treating it like a black box. Recalling advice from an engineering mentor that "You can just use the framework, but a great engineer will really understand the framework" , Billy explained that building a harness yourself is the best way to debug what happens when an agent breaks. You can evaluate three core design decisions for every workflow: Looping : How many iterations should the agent run, and what conditions trigger an exit state? Tools : What specific tools should the agent access, and when and how should it invoke them? Memory : How important is conversational and operational memory, and when should it be retrieved or compacted? Linear Agent Harness: Deterministic Single-Pass Execution Timestamp: [ 21:34 ] Billy demonstrated a minimalist linear harness designed for deterministic workflows where looping is unnecessary. This pattern is ideal for targeted inspections, file transformations, or single-turn data analyses where you want a high level of determinism and need the agent to perform the exact same execution flow every single time. Closed-Loop Agent Harness: Iterative Test-Driven Repair Timestamp: [ 22:45 ] When tasks demand active bug fixing and refactoring, a closed-loop harness provides the iterative reasoning required to reach a verified resolution. In this demo, Billy showcased an agent that applies an automated code edit to address a failing requirement, and the harness executes the unit test suite against the updated codebase. If the tests fail, the runtime captures standard failure logs and detailed stack traces, feeding those error diagnostics directly back into the agent's working memory. The process repeats continuously until all unit tests pass, backed by a five-iteration ceiling to prevent infinite loops and runaway execution costs. Guardrail Harness with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) Timestamp: [ 23:25 ] For developers who require custom behavior without rewriting core orchestration plumbing from scratch, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) provides scaffolding with automated memory management and execution safeguards. Billy walked through an example that leverages ADK's native context compaction to summarize older conversational turns, preventing context window bloat during extended debugging runs. Custom interception hooks inspect and filter shell actions before execution, automatically stopping high-risk operations such as recursive file deletions, database drops, or unauthorized remote git pushes. This architecture gives teams fine-grained control over tool execution boundaries while avoiding the maintenance burden of bespoke harness frameworks. The 3-Layer Agent Dev Stack: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google Antigravity, and Google Skills Timestamp: [ 25:27 ] Next up, Smitha Kolan broke down why coding agents do not always require heavier reasoning models, emphasizing that high performance stems from balancing the three layers of the agent stack: Model , Harness , and Knowledge . "Your coding agent doesn't need a smarter model. It needs a better stack: model, harness, and knowledge. When all three click into place, everything changes." She then walked through the three tools she's been loving recently, one for each layer of the stack. Layer 1 | Model | Gemini 3.8 Flash : High-frequency agentic loops run between 20 and 60 sequential hops per task (inspecting files, updating functions, and executing unit tests). Because latency and API costs compound across iterations, a lightweight, responsive model like Gemini 3.8 Flash makes real-time agent loops practical without running up a massive bill. Layer 2 | Harness | Google Antigravity with /boost : Default Antigravity handles standard navigation and component creation. On top of that, the /boost command spins up an orchestrator that coordinates specialized sub-agents in parallel and concludes with an independent audit pass before modifying files. Layer 3 | Knowledge | Google Skills Repository : With over 19,000 GitHub stars and 100+ curated domain packages across Google Cloud, Firebase, Flutter, and Maps, this harness-agnostic repository injects precise domain context on demand, preventing agents from guessing cloud configurations Your turn to build Building effective coding agents requires moving past the reflex of simply swapping in larger models. As Ryan Lopopolo's philosophy of harness engineering illustrates, true developer leverage is achieved by shifting best practices to the left and investing in rich tools, deterministic verifiers, and well-curated context that survive model upgrades. When combined with fast inference models, structured orchestration harnesses, and modular domain knowledge, agents evolve from conversational novelties into dependable, autonomous engineering partners. Ready to put it into practice? Explore the tools and resources covered in this episode: Gemini 3.8 Flash : Fast, low-cost model for multi-hop agent loops. Google Antigravity ( /boost ): Orchestrator harness for parallel coding agents and verification. Google Skills : Modular domain knowledge for Google Cloud, Firebase, and Flutter. Agent Development Kit (ADK) : Custom harness middleware for safety guardrails and memory compaction. Full episode video : The full interview and live Factory Floor code demos. piezas.titulo: ScyllaDB in Enterprise Java: High-Performance NoSQL With Eclipse JNoSQL
piezas.resumenOriginal: Modern enterprise applications must process increasing data volumes while guaranteeing low latency, high availability, and predictable performance. While relational databases are essential for transactional workloads and complex queries, some applications do not fit the relational model. Systems that manage millions of user engagements, financial events, or IoT data often need a persistence solution built for distributed environments and horizontal scalability. In these cases, ScyllaDB affords a compelling option for enterprise architects. ScyllaDB is a high-performance, distributed NoSQL database based on the wide-column data model. Inspired by Apache Cassandra and compatible with its query language (CQL), ScyllaDB uses a shard-per-core architecture to maximize hardware efficiency and preserve consistent performance under intensive workloads. When should ScyllaDB be chosen over traditional relational databases or other NoSQL options? This article examines its column-family model, compares it with Cassandra, and shows how to integrate ScyllaDB into a Java enterprise application.

piezas.titulo: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense
piezas.resumenOriginal: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense STAR Admin Fri, 02/17/2023 - 20:50 Join STAR Institute and some of its expert clinicians for three nights of learning as we explore the keys to a sensory-informed life. Each night, STAR's Clinical Director will be joined by a different STAR therapist to share tips and strategies around some of families' most often asked questions including: “How can I support and be there for my family when I am constantly feeling burned out?” “What can I do to help my child transition from thing to thing/place to place more smoothly?" “We feel like we walk on egg shells around our child. Why is that and what can we do?" Each night will begin with a 30-40 minute conversation led by the therapist before a live Q&A where you can ask STAR’s occupational therapists and mental health providers your own questions. Discussions You Don't Want to Miss: Caring for Yourself So You Can Care for Others Keys to Successful Transitions in Life’s Big and Small Moments Beyond Fight, Flight, or Freeze: How to Support Regulation STAR Voices You'll Hear From: Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L (she/her) Clinical Director Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L has been a practicing pediatric occupational therapist for over 25 years. She received her BSc in Occupational Therapy from the University of Southern California (USC) in 1996 and her MSW from the University of California-Los Angeles (UCLA) in 2012. She has received advanced training in sensory integration (SIPT certification, STAR ProCert1, STAR ProCert2), listening therapy (Therapeutic Listening, iLs), feeding therapy (SOS), DIR, mental health (DC:0-5 Diagnostic Classification of Mental Health Disorders of Infancy and Early Childhood), and infant massage (CIMI). Her work in occupational therapy with children and youth has occurred in a variety of settings including early intervention, school based, clinic based, mental health and private practice. As a social worker, she provided case management, program development, and program management. Mim has taught both university level (California State-Dominguez Hills) and professional continuing education courses since 2013, spoken internationally, and has co-authored works for professional publications. She has been in her current role at STAR Institute since 2017 at the invitation of Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, PhD, FAOTA, OTR. Gina Crites, OTR/L, MFTC Counselor Gina has a Master’s degree in Marriage and Family Therapy from the University of New Hampshire (2009). She currently provides therapy to individuals (8 years through adulthood), couples, and families in-person or through telehealth (Colorado residents only). Clients would describe Gina’s style as reflective, collaborative, and experiential. She has a calm yet dynamic presence and works from a compassionate, curious, and empowering stance. Gina’s practice is rooted in attachment and systems theories, making her truly a relationally focused therapist. As such, she believes that our greatest healing occurs in the context of relationships. She has always been oriented toward a biopsychosocial approach to her theory of change, thereby honoring the importance of the mind-body connection. She believes that within a safe space and through our attuned relationship with Self and others, we all have the power to tune into our instinct towards healing. With her early career in occupational therapy, Gina has incredible understanding of the importance of self-determination for clients: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. This—coupled with her deep understanding of sensory integration and processing and the importance of occupational roles—truly sets her apart. Her practice honors and respects each person’s unique history and individual differences, and sets clients up for experiencing a deeper sense of self and relational health, on the clients’ own terms. Gina was drawn to couples and family therapy for its non-pathologizing approach to viewing clients’ problems. While biological factors certainly play a role, so do clients’ experiences within their families, partnerships, and larger society. She is passionate about empowering parents to reflect on and integrate their own experiences in service of their children’s health and wellness, as well as their own. “Society does not prioritize proactively supporting its members’ health and therefore, parents and families are not set up for success. This is particularly true for oppressed groups, the poorly included and the disenfranchised.” She believes that parents innately know how high the stakes are and are doing their best, and, like all of us, only benefit from being and feeling less alone in their pain and struggle. Gina is especially equipped to support neurodivergent individuals, couples and families, as well as those navigating issues around disability and chronic illness. She is capable of easily moving between deep therapeutic work, parent coaching and individual skills training - making her a versatile therapist. She has experience supporting clients with life transitions, anxiety, depression, non-suicidal self-harm, suicidal ideation, recovery from adverse childhood experiences and trauma, developing deeper emotional awareness, identifying and leaving behind maladaptive coping patterns, and improving self-esteem. Above all, Gina is a sensory informed, neurodiversity affirming and LGBTQIA+ allied, culturally sensitive and attachment-focused therapist with a special interest in interpersonal neurobiology who strongly believes in the healing power of making sense of our experiences in the context of relationships where we feel seen, heard, and understood. Jayna Niblock, PhD, OTD, OTR/L, BCP Occupational Therapist Jayna graduated from Simpson College with a bachelor's degree in biology and Spanish. She then completed a doctorate in occupational therapy at Creighton University. Jayna was the first Occupational Therapy Pediatric Resident (now called Fellowship) with Creighton University following her occupational therapy degree. During this time, she received advanced training in Sensory Integration and Processing, feeding, the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, and education. Jayna has worked in a variety of pediatric settings prior to coming to STAR Institute and is Board Certified in Pediatrics through the American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA). She currently serves as the Technology Coordinator for the Sensory Integration and Processing Special Interest Section for the AOTA. Jayna enjoys engaging in play-based therapy focused on relationship building between a child and their family. She brings a strengths-based approach to support the child and family achieve their goals in life. Jayna has advanced training in Sensory Integration and Processing differences including Mentorship Certification through the STAR Institute. She is also trained in Integrated Listening Systems (iLS) and the Sequential Oral Sensory (SOS) approach to feeding. Jayna has a Doctor of Philosophy in Educational Leadership and seeks to support practice through research and evidence. Jayna is an ally to the neurodiverse community and strives to learn more and integrate practices which support neurodiverse persons to build a strong sense of self and live their most sensory-rich lives. Chelsea Marquette, (COTA/L) Licensed Certified Occupational Therapy Assistant Chelsea graduated with her Bachelor of Science in Family Studies and Human Services from Kansas State University in 2014 and then in 2018 graduated from Pueblo Community College with an Associate of Applied Science Occupational Therapy Assistant. Since 2018 she has worked in multidisciplinary team pediatric outpatient settings and post-acute care rehab with adults. She has supervised four OTA students and in May 2022 presented for OTAC on social emotional development in children and teens with her past supervising OTR. Chelsea enjoys building relationships with families and helping them find joy together. Her special interests include providing trauma-informed and neurodiverse-affirming care. She has taken courses to expand her understanding of trauma through the Starr Commonwealth and with Bessel van der Kolk. She has also taken the Learn Play Thrive Approach to Autism course. She is a member of AOTA and enjoys learning more to become a better OTA. During her free time, Chelsea likes soaking up the sunshine, reading, yoga, and going to museums. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. AI-generated avatars explain concepts The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material. Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions. Modeling expert reasoning through dialogue The cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance. Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team. A new standard for advanced engineering education By merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. piezas.titulo: Pediatric brain charts reveal ADHD biotypes with distinct developmental, molecular, and therapeutic profiles
piezas.resumenOriginal: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibits profound clinical heterogeneity; however, its underlying neurobiological substrates remain unclear. Here, leveraging large - scale structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 12,663 typically developing children and 1,699 children with ADHD across Chinese and United States cohorts, we construct population specific pediatric brain charts via hierarchical Bayesian normative modeling to quantify individual deviations in cortical morphology. Data-driven clustering identifies two robust, cross - ethnically replicable ADHD biotypes: an infra - normal biotype characterized by widespread cortical thinning and a supra - normal biotype marked by cortical thickening. Multivariate analyses reveal distinct brain-behavior architectures: cortical deviations correlate preferentially with symptom severity in the infra-normal biotype but with both symptom severity and cognitive performance in the supranormal biotype. Clinically, the infra-normal biotype demonstrates a superior response to methylphenidate over atomoxetine, whereas the supra-normal biotype responds comparably to both. Transcriptomic analyses identify biotype-specific molecular signatures converging with ADHD genome-wide association study (GWAS) risk loci but exhibiting distinct expression patterns in the brain. These findings classify ADHD heterogeneity into neurobiologically distinct, clinically informed biotypes, providing a mechanistic framework for precision psychiatry in pediatric ADHD.

piezas.titulo: Preoperative cranial computed tomography in pediatric cochlear implantation: clinical necessity or optional step?
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectivesDue to growing evidence regarding the risks of ionizing radiation, especially in children, some centers now perform cochlear implantation (CI) without a preoperative computed tomography (CT) scan, relying solely on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This study evaluates the necessity and safety of omitting CT scans before bilateral CI in children.MethodsA retrospective analysis of 164 children, implanted bilaterally between 2018 and 2024 and aged under 10 years at the time of either simultaneous or second CI, were included. The impact of preoperative imaging on duration of surgery and perioperative complications was analyzed. The surgical procedure was compared between cases with and without a preoperative CT scan and analyzed for surgeons in training and experienced surgeons.Results105 children were implanted with a preoperative CT scan and 59 without a CT scan. The duration of bilateral CI surgery was 122.5 (±41.4) min for procedures [CI without CT: 122.5 (±41.4) min; CI with CT: 116.1 (±33.84) min; (p = 0.4861)] and anesthesia [CI without CT: 237.2 (±47.38) min; CI with CT: 226.3 (±41.50) min; (p = 0.1352)] did not differ significantly between the groups, irrespective of the experience of the surgeons. Seven cases showed relevant malformations visible on MRI, such as large vestibular aqueduct syndrome, which were relevant during the surgery. Minor and major complications occurred rarely in both cohorts but more frequently in patients without CT scan (without CT: 10.2% (6/59); with CT: 4.8% (5/105); p = 0.2052; risk difference [RD], 5.4%; 95% CI, −6.3 to 14.3%). Intraoperative X-ray imaging revealed no cases of electrode tip fold-over, and no patients developed postoperative complete or incomplete facial nerve palsy.ConclusionIn summary, an MRI-based imaging strategy without routine preoperative CT may be safe and sufficient in appropriately selected pediatric CI candidates, with additional CT reserved for patients in whom clinical or MRI findings suggest relevant bony abnormalities, complex inner ear malformations, or syndromic conditions. This approach reduces unnecessary radiation exposure and the use of healthcare resources, while avoiding redundant diagnostic information from both imaging modalities, without compromising surgical safety or outcomes.

piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

piezas.titulo: Early development of cerebellar functional connectivity
piezas.resumenOriginal: The cerebellum makes a critical contribution to cognitive and behavioural function, extending well beyond motor control, and is recognised as an important determinant of neurodevelopmental outcome. Despite this, little is known about the foundations of cerebellar functional organisation in early life. Addressing this gap is essential for establishing typical developmental trajectories against which atypical development can be assessed. Here, we analysed fMRI data from term-born neonates (n=155) scanned between 37 and 44 weeks postmenstrual age and mapped intra-cerebellar and cerebro-cerebellar functional connectivity across multiple levels of organisation. We identified 13 intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) within the neonatal cerebellum that recapitulated adult subdivisions, with two ICNs showing age-related increases in coverage and strength. Analysis of cerebro-cerebellar connectivity identified 15 sensory, motor and association cerebral clusters, seven increasing connectivity with age. Functional gradient analysis identified a continuous axis from somatomotor to association regions within intra-cerebellar and cerebro-cerebellar organisation, which became more pronounced with age. Together, these findings suggest that the foundations of adult cerebellar functional organisation are present at birth but undergo rapid and regionally heterogeneous maturation over the first weeks of postnatal life. This developmental framework provides a normative reference for understanding cerebellar development and its implications for later neurodevelopmental variation.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. piezas.titulo: Are clinician-administered ataxia scales truly culture-free? Rethinking contextual validity in diverse populations
piezas.resumenOriginal: Hereditary cerebellar ataxias are genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous progressive neurodegenerative disorders characterized by substantial functional impairment. With the emergence of disease-modifying therapies and gene-targeted clinical trials, standardized and reliable clinical outcome measures are essential for assessing disease severity and progression. Among the available scales, two are widely used by clinicians to assess ataxia: The Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) and the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS). Given considerable linguistic, educational and sociocultural heterogeneity across the globe, we opine that it may pose challenges to the uniform application and cross-cultural comparability of these instruments. Published translations and adaptations were also examined to determine whether cultural adaptation extended beyond linguistic translation. Among all the identified adaptations, reported processes predominantly comprised forward and backward translation, expert review and assessment of linguistic, conceptual or cultural equivalence. These findings suggest that linguistic translation alone may not be sufficient to ensure that clinician-rated ataxia scales retain equivalent meaning and measurement across diverse populations. We therefore introduce the concept of “contextual validity” emphasizing that language, educational heterogeneity, literacy, graphomotor familiarity, cultural practices and testing environments that may influence performance independently of cerebellar dysfunction. This perspective outlines considerations for developing contextually adapted and psychometrically validated Indian-language versions of SARA and ICARS to improve measurement accuracy and support equitable clinical assessment and participation in global clinical trials.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de puntuación: la validez contextual también influye. Las escalas de ataxia SARA e ICARS, aunque traducidas, pueden fallar en poblaciones con distinta educación y costumbres. Adaptarlas al idioma y cultura india podría mejorar la precisión en ensayos globales.

Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2023-50431) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 09/12/2023 Fecha de última actualización: 16/10/2026 sec_attest_info en drivers/accel/habanalabs/common/habanalabs_ioctl.c en el kernel de Linux hasta 6.6.5 permite una fuga de información al espacio del usuario porque info->pad0 no está inicializado. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2024-0607) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 18/01/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 16/10/2026 Se encontró una falla en el subsistema Netfilter en el kernel de Linux. El problema está en la función nft_byteorder_eval(), donde el código itera a través de un bucle y escribe en la matriz `dst`. En cada iteración, se escriben 8 bytes, pero `dst` es una matriz de u32, por lo que cada elemento solo tiene espacio para 4 bytes. Eso significa que cada iteración sobrescribe parte del elemento anterior, lo que posiblemente lleve a una escritura fuera de los límites. Esta falla permite que un usuario local provoque una denegación de servicio o potencialmente aumente sus privilegios en el sistema. Vulnerabilidad en m2crypto (CVE-2023-50781) Severidad: ALTA Fecha de publicación: 05/02/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 15/10/2026 Se encontró una falla en m2crypto. Este problema puede permitir que un atacante remoto descifre mensajes capturados en servidores TLS que utilizan intercambios de claves RSA, lo que puede provocar la exposición de datos confidenciales o sensibles. Vulnerabilidad en kernel de Linux (CVE-2024-35809) Severidad: MEDIA Fecha de publicación: 17/05/2024 Fecha de última actualización: 15/10/2026 En el kernel de Linux, se ha resuelto la siguiente vulnerabilidad: PCI/PM: drena las devoluciones de llamada inactivas en tiempo de ejecución antes de eliminar el controlador. Una condición de ejecución entre la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() y la devolución de llamada .remove() en el controlador PCI rtsx_pcr conduce a un crash de kernel debido a un error de página no controlado [1]. El problema es que no se espera que rtsx_pci_runtime_idle() se ejecute después de llamar a pm_runtime_get_sync(), pero esto último realmente no garantiza eso. Solo garantiza que las devoluciones de llamada de suspensión y reanudación no se ejecutarán cuando regrese. Sin embargo, si ya se está ejecutando una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() cuando se llama a pm_runtime_get_sync(), este último notará que el estado de PM en tiempo de ejecución del dispositivo es RPM_ACTIVE y regresará de inmediato sin esperar a que se complete el primero. De hecho, no puede esperar a que se complete .runtime_idle() porque puede ser llamado desde esa devolución de llamada (podría decirse que no tiene mucho sentido hacerlo, pero no está estrictamente prohibido). Por lo tanto, en general, quien proporciona una devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() debe protegerla para que no se ejecute en paralelo con cualquier código que se ejecute después de pm_runtime_get_sync(). [Tenga en cuenta que .runtime_idle() no se iniciará después de que pm_runtime_get_sync() haya regresado, pero puede continuar ejecutándose si comenzó antes.] Una forma de abordar esa condición de ejecución es llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() después de pm_runtime_get_sync() (no antes porque es necesario un valor distinto de cero del contador de uso de PM en tiempo de ejecución para evitar que se invoquen devoluciones de llamada de PM en tiempo de ejecución) para esperar a que se complete la devolución de llamada .runtime_idle() en caso de que se esté ejecutando en ese punto. Un lugar adecuado para hacerlo es pci_device_remove() que llama a pm_runtime_get_sync() antes de eliminar el controlador, por lo que también puede llamar a pm_runtime_barrier() posteriormente, lo que evitará que se produzca la ejecución en cuestión, no sólo en el controlador rtsx_pcr, sino en cualquier controlador PCI que proporcione devoluciones de llamada .runtime_idle(). Esta falla solo se manifiesta si el archivo netrc tiene una entrada `default` que omite tanto el nombre de usuario como la contraseña. Una circunstancia poco común. piezas.resumenOriginal: A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

piezas.titulo: Differential value processing in the rostral and causal subthalamic nucleus during flexible and habitual decision-making in primates: Implications for cognitive dysfunction in Parkinson's disease
piezas.resumenOriginal: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) is a major target region of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD), effectively alleviating motor symptoms. However, STN-DBS can also induce cognitive impairments, suggesting that the STN contributes to cognitive functions beyond simple motor control. Furthermore, anatomical organization supports functional segregation of cognitive processes, as basal ganglia subregions encoding flexible and stable values topographically project to distinct STN subregions. Yet, whether the STN contributes to cognitive functions and, if so, how subregions of the STN differentially process cognitive flexibility and habitual stability remains unknown. Here, we reveal a rostral-caudal functional organization of the STN that differentially supports flexible value updating and long-term value memory, enabling adaptive and habitual decision-making, respectively. Neurons in the rostral STN (rSTN) preferentially encode flexibly updated values, whereas neurons in the caudal STN (cSTN) preferentially encode stable long-term value memories. Notably, inactivation of the STN along the rostral-caudal axis produced dissociable behavioral deficits: rSTN inactivation selectively impaired goal-directed behavior requiring flexible value updating, whereas cSTN inactivation selectively disrupted habitual behavior guided by long-term value memories. Together, these results reveal a rostral-caudal functional segregation of the STN, with the rSTN supporting goal-directed behavior and the cSTN supporting habitual behavior. These findings further provide a framework for understanding how STN dysfunction or STN-DBS in Parkinson's disease may differentially affect cognitive processes beyond motor control.

piezas.titulo: From virtual practice to real-world function the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation
piezas.resumenOriginal: Digital technologies have expanded opportunities for neurorehabilitation by enabling intensive, interactive, and adaptable motor practice. However, improvements achieved within virtual environments, rehabilitation games, or technology-based assessments do not necessarily translate into meaningful changes in everyday function. This Mini Review examines the transfer problem in digital neurorehabilitation and discusses key factors that may limit the generalization of training-related gains to real-world performance. We synthesize evidence regarding task specificity, sensory and perception-action differences between digital and physical environments, cognitive and contextual demands, practice variability, and patient-specific constraints that influence transfer. Based on these mechanisms, we propose a transfer-oriented framework consisting of five interconnected stages: skill acquisition, adaptive variability, cognitive-motor integration, contextualized real-world practice, and ecological evaluation. This framework emphasizes that transfer should be deliberately targeted rather than assumed as a consequence of successful digital training. We further discuss how virtual reality, augmented reality, wearable sensing, and hybrid rehabilitation models may support different stages of this process when integrated within adaptive and personalized approaches. Future digital rehabilitation research should move beyond evaluating performance within trained tasks and incorporate measures of functional and ecological transfer, including real-world mobility, activity, and participation. A shift from technology-centered rehabilitation toward transfer-oriented design may enhance the clinical impact of digital interventions and support meaningful improvements in daily life.

piezas.titulo: State-dependent responses of emotional brain networks in high myopia under blurred vision: a shift towards dorsal stream and cross-modal processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: PurposeReliable sensory input plays a vital role in shaping emotional experience, however, how the brain modulates the formation of emotion under chronic visual degradation remains unclear. Using high myopia (HM) as a natural model of sustained blur, this study investigated state-dependent responses of emotional brain networks during blurred movie viewing.MethodsTwenty-four participants with high myopia (HM) were tested without optical correction, comparing with normal vision (NV) controls from previous research. All participants watched thriller and scenic movie clips twice over one week during fMRI. Intra-subject synchrony and seed-based functional connectivity analyses focused on the amygdala and visual processing streams.ResultsCompared to NV controls, the HM group exhibited reduced intra-subject synchrony in visual cortices but increased synchrony in the primary auditory cortex, indicating cross-modal compensatory enhancement. During threat processing, HM participants showed strengthened and stable functional connectivity between the amygdala and the dorsal visual stream. For non-threatening content, this enhanced connectivity initially involved both dorsal and ventral stream but persisted selectively in the dorsal stream upon repeated viewing.ConclusionSustained visual blur elicits a perceptual-state-dependent functional response in emotional networks, characterized by heightened cross-modal auditory integration and an increased recruitment of the visual dorsal stream during blurred viewing. These findings highlight the brain’s immediate compensatory mechanisms under conditions of ambiguous visual input.

piezas.titulo: Textures are less comfortable to view than other natural images, consistent with cortical hyper-metabolism theory
piezas.resumenOriginal: Images considered uncomfortable to view often over-represent mid-range spatial frequencies (mid-SFs) relative to the average 1/f amplitude spectrum of natural images. A proposed mechanism for this discomfort known as the Cortical Hyper-metabolism Hypothesis (CHH) posits that such images over-activate the visual cortex, which is highly sensitive to mid-SFs. We tested a novel prediction of the CHH, namely that natural image categories like textures which over-represent mid-SFs will be less comfortable to view on average than other natural images. We indeed found that texture images were less comfortable to view than various non-textures, validating this prediction of the CHH and demonstrating its potential relevance to natural image aesthetics. Passing our images through models of early visual neurons demonstrated that the mean activity of a population of simulated log-Gabor filters resembling V1 simple cells best predicted discomfort. Manipulations which selectively altered the image phase or amplitude spectra while leaving the other intact were less comfortable than the originals, suggesting that visual comfort is not a simple function of either one of these characteristics. Our results suggest that although many factors contribute to the visual comfort of natural image categories, early visual processing may play an important role, consistent with the CHH.

piezas.titulo: From Arm to Leg: A Shared Primitive Framework for Solving Inverse Kinematics in Human Movement
piezas.resumenOriginal: In motor control, the idea of a modular control architecture has been repeatedly discussed. This framework has been widely applied to kinematic and kinetic data, primarily to examine how the central nervous system (CNS) controls multiple elements simultaneously and how it handles redundant or excessive degrees of freedom. However, the inverse kinematics problem, traditionally defined as the mapping from a desired task-space outcome to the corresponding joint-space solution, has usually been treated separately from this framework. Recent work from our laboratory suggests that modular control may directly address all these problems by relying on a shared low-dimensional primitive space common to internal and external movement representations, as supported by recent studies of human hand-drawing kinematics. In the present study, we extended this framework from upper-limb drawing to lower-limb gait kinematics. We also used it to explore how different CNS pathologies may alter the organization of movement within this shared space. Overall, this study investigates whether walking, like other forms of movement, can be understood as arising from a small number of underlying primitives that are flexibly combined across coordinate systems.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

piezas.titulo: An exploratory study of relationships between the executive functions and spatiotemporal control in a complex motor task: the spatial tapping task
piezas.resumenOriginal: Executive functions (EFs) are cognitive processes enabling planning, control, and regulation of behavior. A variety of tasks have been developed to evaluate EFs, from complex reasoning to simpler inhibition tasks, reflecting the diversity of symptoms observed in patients with executive deficits. Recent research has emphasized their unity, proposing three core functions, working memory, inhibition, and switching, that share resources and combine to enable complex tasks. Yet, no single task captures both the unity and diversity of EFs, limiting the development of a unified framework and a balanced assessment. To address this gap, we designed the spatial tapping task, a timing paradigm combining finger tapping and circle drawing. Finger tapping requires working memory for explicit timing control, whereas circle drawing requires anticipatory control akin to switching to control movement trajectory, enabling implicit timing control. Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. A slow tempo favors discrete movements with long pauses between taps, whereas a fast tempo promotes continuous motion. Previous analyses supported a change in timing control mode with increasing tempo. Here, we explored the hypothesis that EFs are engaged accordingly: working memory in the slow/discrete phase, switching in the fast/continuous phase, and inhibition in the intermediate phase, where demands for continuous motion increase. In two studies combined into a single dataset, we compared scores with those from neuropsychological tests using correlations. We found that timing accuracy in the slow/discrete phase was associated with working memory, spatial accuracy in the fast/continuous phase with switching, and longer contact time in the intermediate phase with inhibition. We also explored whether performance was consistent with the EF deficits described in the literature, and the potential contribution of motor output, reporting scores obtained across populations with executive deficits (aging and dementia), combined executive and motor impairments (schizophrenia), and motor expertise (biscriptual writers), along with matched controls. Findings were consistent, although often more specific, and highlighted an important contribution of motor output. Altogether, our results provide initial evidence that the task can be used to investigate EFs, although cognitive, motor, and sensory contributions need to be disentangled to improve its specificity.

destilado.texto: No es solo cuestión de fuerza: también de tiempo, pues las funciones ejecutivas se activan según el ritmo del tapping espacial. En la fase lenta se vinculan con la memoria de trabajo, en la rápida con el cambio de estrategia, y en la intermedia con la inhibición, según datos de Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. ¿Podrá este patrón guiar evaluaciones motoras más equilibradas?
